sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Due to their unique activity towards formation of alcohols and hydrocarbons, copper (Cu) based catalysts have
been widely used in the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (ERCD). Cu foam naturally possesses three-dimensional (3D) porous structure and catalytically active Cu elements, exhibiting very good catalytic ability for ERCD. Herein, nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes with Cu foam as the substrate, with progressive morphologies of nanowires (CuNW), nanosheets (CuNS) and nanoflowers (CuNF), are in-situ prepared by simply adjusting the reaction time in a strongly alkaline oxidizing solution. It is found that the performance and products distribution of ERCD are affected by both the morphology of the as prepared nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes and the electrolyte species. As electrode micromorphology evolves from nanowire to nanoflower, the initial electrode potential required for C2 products generation shifts to more positive values. The CuNS electrode shows the highest Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 86.9% at -0.4 V (vs. RHE) and superior performance, owing to its nanosheet morphology that can better stabilize the intermediate state products. Moreover, both total FE and products distribution are affected by the electrolyte anion species. The highest total FE in the investigated electrolyte on CuNS electrode obeys the following order: KHCO3 (86.9%, -0.4 V (vs. RHE)) > KCl (54.7%, -0.5 V (vs. RHE)) > KH2PO4 (1.0%, -0.9 V (vs. RHE)). In 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3, the CuNS electrode shows a very complex products distribution; in 1.0 mol·L-1 KCl, the products distribution can be feasibly controlled by the applied potential; while in 1.0 mol-1·L KH2PO4, ERCD is almost totally suppressed by hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). It is the first time that the CuNS electrodes are applied for ERCD with low cost, simple synthesis, easy scale-up and high activity. Combined with the flexible control ability in FE and product distributions, CuNS electrode possesses great potential for the industrial application of ERCD. Keywords: Electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide; Electrode (micro) morphology; Self-supporting Cu electrode; Products distribution control.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The development of economy has led to the increasing consumption of fossil fuels, and thus
causing excessive emission of CO2 in the atmosphere, which is primarily responsible for most drastic environmental issues, such as global warming, greenhouse effect and climate deterioration [1, 2]. On the other hand, CO2 is the most abundant and the least expensive C1 resource. Converting CO2 through a clean way can not only curtail CO2 but also obtain value-added feedbacks. Several strategies, such as photocatalytic reduction, electrocatalytic reduction and thermocatalytic conversion of CO2 have been widely studied [3, 4]. Among of them, electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ERCD) into low-carbon species (CO, CH4, CH3OH, HCOOH etc.) through electricity generated by sustainable energies such as wind and solar energy has been proposed as a promising solution [5, 6]. This process can store these clean but hard-to-transport energies locally as well as mitigate environmental issues by converting CO2 into useful hydrocarbons. It is also attractive for its high-energy efficiency, controllable and flexible reaction system and environmentally benign properties.
Since CO2 is an extremely stable molecule, its conversion into useful products needs tough
requirements for efficient catalysts and sufficient energy input [7]. It is well-known that the catalyst type and electrolyte characteristics play an important role in the performance and consequent products distribution of ERCD [8, 9]. Toward ERCD, various kinds of catalysts have been investigated, including metals, carbon materials and some molecule catalysts [10]. It is generally believed that ERCD performance is essentially related to the intrinsic properties of catalysts. On Sn, Pb, In, Hg and Bi, ECRD tends to generate HCOOH [11-12], while on noble metals like Pd, Au, and Ag, CO is favorable to be produced [13]. Carbon materials such as graphene, carbon nanotubes and carbon quantum dots also show their preference for CO and HCOOH [14].While Cu is found to be the
3
only one capable of producing hydrocarbons in a more considerable efficiency than CO and HCOOH from ECRD [15]. Molecular catalysts are some metal complexes, such as Cu, Ni and Co complexes. On these molecular catalysts, the products distribution of ECRD mainly depends on the central metal atoms and their molecular structures [16-18]. Besides, the morphology and composition of catalysts can affect the ERCD performance [19, 20]. Furthermore, the type of electrolytes also have some effects on the ERCD performance largely. Up to now, KHCO3 is usually adopted to promote the CO2 diffusion process, since the solubility of CO2 is only 0.33 mol L -1 in water [21, 22]; the other electrolytes with halogens such as KCl KI, and KBr have also been investigated [23]. Moreover, ERCD involves complex electron transfer and reaction processes, making it extremely difficult to control a specific reaction pathway. ERCD to CO and HCOOH is a two-electron process, which has a more facile kinetic. While, for the formation of alcohols and hydrocarbons, the multi-electron processes undergo a high overpotential and sluggish kinetic [24].
Achieving high efficiency in value-added and high-energy dense products, such as hydrocarbons
and alcohols, is crucial for the application of ERCD in energy storage, transportation and the chemical industry, which has been a fundamental goal for ERCD. Copper-based materials are considered as the most promising catalysts for this goal. Rahaman et al. [25] reported that electrodeposited Cu dendrites showed high selectivity towards formate and C2H4 production at lower and higher overpotentials, respectively. The oxides derived Cu catalysts presented a remarkably high selectivity towards ethanol (FEEtOH (Faradaic efficiency) = 13.0% at -1.0 V (vs. RHE)) and n-propanol (FEn-PrOH = 13.1% at -0.9 V (vs. RHE)) production. Ren et al. [26] reported that at copper (I) oxide catalysts CO2 was reduced to ethylene and ethanol, and the FE of ethylene and ethanol could be systematically tuned by adjusting the thickness of the deposited overlayers. Song et al. [27] found that Cu nanoparticles with a highly textured, N-doped carbon nanospike film converted CO2 directly
4
into ethanol with both high FE (63% at -1.2 V (vs. RHE)) and high selectivity (84%).
As reported, morphology and surface composition of the Cu based catalysts as well as the
electrolyte characteristics have certain influence on ERCD performance. Cu based catalysts with different morphologies, such as nanoparticle, nanowire, and nanocube, had been widely investigated, and products distribution related to the reaction paths varied with morphologies [28]. It was found that oxygen species in surface and subsurface regions of the Cu catalysts played a vital role in the activity and selectivity of ERCD. Oxygen species could affect the oxidation state of the surface layer (or near region), and thus create defects and improve the roughness when removed, resulting in the variation of the ERCD performance [29]. The pH and the species of electrolyte are also crucial for the ERCD. The pH value exerts a great influence on product selectivity [30]. Some cations and anions in electrolytes could facilitate the CO2 adsorption and stabilize one of the possible intermediates and finally promote ERCD [31-33].
However, most reported Cu based catalysts still face the challenges of complicated and difficult
preparation processes, high price and low activity. Besides, their corresponding reaction mechanism remains vague. These challenges still hinder the industrialization of ERCD. As known, Cu foam naturally possesses 3D porous structure and can be easily modified. Through in-situ technique, which is a kind of simple, efficient and cheap way for material synthesis, Cu foam can be controllably, efficiently, and massively modified into a highly active, low cost self-supporting electrode.
In this study, three kinds of nanostructured self-supporting Cu-based-electrodes with nanowire,
nanosheet and nanoflower morphologies were in-situ prepared from Cu foam by the impregnation method and in-situ reduced to metallic Cu by cyclic voltammetry (CV). The effects of electrode morphology and electrolyte on ERCD performance were investigated, and a hypothesis on the ERCD
5
mechanism on CuNS electrode was formulated. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first time that electrodes based on Cu foam with well-controlled progressive micro-morphology were in-situ fabricated, and the Cu nanosheets were for first time investigated for ERCD.

sections.heading: 2.1 Preparation of nanostructured Cu catalysts
sections.text:
All chemicals used in this work were of analytical grade without further purification. The
Cu foam (Changjia, China) was firstly sheared into 1.0 cm×2.0 cm pieces and subsequently treated with a 6.0 mol·L-1 HCl aqueous solution, ethanol and deionized water through sonication for 30 min. K2S2O8 (0.68 g) and NaOH (2.50 g) were separately dissolved in deionized water and finally mixed with each other to make up a 50.0 mL solution as the oxidizing agent. Then the as treated Cu foam species were immersed into the above oxidizing solution at room temperature and remained stationary. This oxidation process was controlled to 20, 120 and 720 min, respectively. Finally, the Cu foam species were removed from the solution, rinsed with deionized water, dried in air and ready for in-situ reduction by CV before ERCD tests.

sections.heading: 2.2 Physico-chemical characterization of nanostructured Cu catalysts
sections.text:
Scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to observe the morphology and structure of
the electrodes with JSM-6330F instruments. The composition of the materials was demonstrated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) using a VG Scientific ESCALAB250 instrument equipped with Al Kα X-ray source (1486.6 eV).

sections.heading: 2.3 Electrochemical tests and products analysis
sections.text:
All electrochemical measurements were conducted in a three-electrode electrochemical H-type
cell connected to a Zennium electrochemical working station (Zahner, Germany), at room
6
temperature and ambient pressure. A proton exchange membrane (Nafion®-117 membrane, DuPont Company) was adopted to separate the cathode and anode cells in order to avoid the oxidation of the eventual products. Aqueous KHCO3, KCl and KH2PO4 solutions with the concentration of 1.0 mol·L-1 were chosen as the electrolytes, respectively. Before tests, all kinds of electrolytes were saturated with CO2 (99.999%). The corresponding pH values of these three electrolytes (KHCO3, KCl and KH2PO4) after saturated with CO2 were 7.5, 5.6 and 3.9, respectively. During the tests, 30.0 mL of the electrolyte was added into both the cathode and anode cell. CO2 was continuously purged into both cells at a flow rate of 20 mL·min-1 to exclude the remnant air and keep the electrolyte saturated with CO2. Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl aqueous solution) was used as the reference electrode, while a Pt sheet was adopted as the counter electrode. The as-prepared nanostructured Cu electrodes were used as the working electrodes. It should be noted that, without specification, all potentials are referred to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), calculated by Eq. (1).
E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 + 0.0591 × pH (1)
The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was conducted with a scan rate of 10 mV·s-1. The CV
treatment was applied to clean the electrode surface and simultaneously reduce the copper oxides, so that the electrodes could remain stable. In Fig. S1, the three-electrode electrochemical system and the products analysis system are schematically represented. Potentiostatic tests were conducted for 40 min in each potential. The oxygen generated at the anode cell was vented out directly into air. The target products generated at the cathode cell were detected and analyzed. The gaseous products were detected and quantitated by online gas chromatography (GC1100 Beijing Persee) equipped with GDX 502 and PQ columns, in which He (99.999%) was adopted as the carrier gas. The TCD detector was used to analyze H2 and CO, and the FID detector was
7
used to analyze CH4, C2H4 and C2H6, respectively. Liquid phase products were analyzed by a 400 MHz NMR (Bruker AVANCE IIIT HD 400 NMR system, Germany) after electrolyzation. To make a sample, 60.0 µL D2O, 500.0 µL liquid phase products and 40.0 µL dimethylsulfoxide (450 ppm aqueous solution) as internal standard were tested to quantify the products. The 1H spectrum was measured with water suppression. The FE for all products is calculated by Eq. (2):
FE = zFn/Q × 100% (2)
where z is the number of transferred electrons, F (C·mol-1) the Faraday constant, n (mol) the amount of the target product, and Q (C) the total quantity of charge in the testing process.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
As clearly seen from the SEM images (Fig. 1), along with the different oxidation time in the
electrodes preparation process, the three electrodes present different morphologies, i.e. nanowires (CuNW) (20 min) (Figs 1a-1b), nanosheets (CuNS) (120 min) (Figs 1c-1d), and nanoflowers (CuNF) (720 min) (Figs 1e-1f), respectively. Moreover, obviously these three nanostructured Cu oxide species are all uniformly coated on the surface of Cu foam. From the higher magnification SEM images (Fig. 1b), it can be clearly seen that in the case of CuNW, the length of nanowires is about ~20 µm with a diameter of ~120 nm. As for CuNS (Fig. 1d), the length of the nanosheet is about ~30 µm and the thickness about ~20 nm. Furthermore, CuNF resembles a pinball structure (Fig. 1f), which is a cluster of nanosheets that grow in a certain direction at certain locations.
These results indicate that the morphology of the nanostructured self-supporting Cu
electrodes is heavily dependent on the oxidation time of Cu foams in the alkaline oxidizing agent. When the reaction time is no more than 10 min, the surface color of the Cu foam gradually becomes dim and the metallic luster disappears. As the oxidation time extends to 10-20 min, a
8
uniform blue film can be gradually formed on the surface of the Cu foam, indicating the formation of CuNW, which has also been previously reported [34].
. When the oxidation time continues to increase to 20-120 min, the blue film gradually
changes into a uniform grey-black film, indicating the formation of CuNS, as verified by SEM results (Figs 1e and 1f). Along with the further increment in the oxidation time for Cu foam, the grey black gradually deepens, indicating the further assemblage of nanoflowers. The above described color change can be seen in Fig. S2.
According to the color of the sample, it can be inferred that the oxidation products on the Cu
foam surface could be Cu(OH)2 and CuO. The corresponding valence state of the nanostructured Cu
9
electrodes is verified by the XPS results (Fig. 2). The high-resolution Cu 2p3/2 spectra of Cu foam are shown in Fig. 2a. The sharp peak at 931.9 eV can be ascribed to Cu0 on the surface of Cu foam.

For the Cu NW, Cu NS and Cu NF, the high resolution Cu 2p3/2 spectra (Figs 2b-2d) can be deconvoluted into two peaks at about 931.9 and 933.5 eV with a two satellite peaks (denoted as “sat.”), corresponding to Cu0 and Cu2+, respectively. The high intense satellite peak implies that a large amount of Cu2+ have been produced at the surface of Cu foam after the oxidation process [35]. More importantly, the binding energy (BE) of Cu 2p3/2 spectra from the Cu NW, Cu NS, and Cu NF shows a negative shift, suggesting that Cu(OH)2 can be efficiently converted into CuO. These results
10
match well with the above mentioned color observation.
Based on the above physico-chemical results, the formation mechanism of the
self-supporting Cu based electrodes might be as follows: when Cu foam is immerged into the strongly alkaline oxidizing solution, the OH- ions in the solution are rapidly and selectively adsorbed onto the Cu foam surface. Simultaneously, the strong oxidation agent of S2O8 2- starts to attack the reductive Cu(0) to form Cu(II), which consequently reacts with OH- to form the blue Copper(II) hydroxide (Cu(OH)2). Then, the as-formed Cu(OH)2 can be gradually assembled into nanowires [36]. As known, Cu(OH)2 is a weakly amphoteric substance and thus it can be slightly soluble in alkaline solution; while copper oxide is insoluble compared with Cu(OH)2.
Consequently, according to the law of the precipitation transformation, Cu(OH)2 can be
gradually transformed into the more insoluble CuO, and thus the surface of Cu foam from blue turns into black color gradually. In the shrinking process, Cu(OH)2 nanowires clump together to form nanosheets. When the oxidation time is further extended, these nanosheets do not further grow but just pile up, and eventually form pine-fruit-shaped nanoflowers [37].
The schematic diagram is given in Fig. 3 and the reaction equations could be as follows:
K2S2O8 + Cu K2SO4 + CuSO4 (3) 2K2S2O8 + 4NaOH 2K2SO4 + 2Na2SO4 + 2H2O + O2 (4) CuSO4 + 2NaOH Cu(OH)2 (Blue) + Na2SO4 (5) Cu(OH)2 CuO (Black) + H2O (6)
11
By comparing the results for Cu(0) oxidation and Cu2+ reduction peaks (Fig. 4a), one can
distinguish that after CV treatment (Fig. 4b), the corresponding reduction peaks of Cu (II) disappear (Fig. 4c), indicating that Cu (II) has been completely converted into Cu(0). It should
12
be noted that, in the validation process (Fig. 4c), in order to avoid the as-obtained Cu(0) through CV treatment to be oxidized again, the upper potential limit is set at the point of 0.395 V, where Cu(0) oxidation has still not started (Fig. 4a). Accordingly, judging from the inexistence of the reduction peak of Cu(II) (Fig. 4c), one can infer that Cu(II) at the Cu foam surface has been completely reduced into Cu(0) after the CV treatment.
The effect of electrodes morphology on ERCD performance was firstly explored by using
As shown, at the raw Cu foam electrode (Fig. 5a), the LSV curves in N2 and CO2 saturated
1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3 electrolyte are crossed at -0.65 V. After -0.65 V, the reduction current
13
density in CO2 saturated electrolyte is a little greater than that in N2 saturated electrolyte, which indicates that pure Cu foam exhibits some ERCD catalytic activity. In fact, hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is much more active dynamically and inevitable at all potentials in an ERCD system, but there is still a potential range that ERCD becomes the dominant reaction. On the other hand, out of this potential range, HER will be the main reaction. At CuNW electrode (Fig. 5b), since -0.3 V, the current density in CO2 saturated electrolyte is obviously higher than that in N2 saturated electrolyte, indicating that the initial reduction potential of ERCD is at about -0.3 V and CuNW electrode exhibits a desirable ERCD activity. By comparing the results in Figs 5c and 5d, it can be seen that CuNS and CuNF exhibit the same behavior towards ERCD as CuNW.
Based on Fig. 5, one can make a further comparison of LSV curves of these four electrodes
in the terms of the initial reduction potential value and current density. As for the initial reduction potential of ERCD is concerned, the raw Cu foam gives a more negative value compared with that of CuNW, CuNS, and CuNF electrode, while the latter three electrodes present almost the same trend. As for their ERCD current density values, especially the D-value (the current density difference at a specific potential between CO2 and N2 saturated electrolytes at the same electrode) of the raw Cu foam is smaller than that of CuNW, CuNS and CuNF electrodes. Moreover, the D-value of the CuNS electrode is the highest in the investigated potential range. Based on the LSV results, it can be easily inferred that the CuNS electrode possesses a better ERCD performance than the others do.
For the further ERCD performance evaluation, the potentiostatic tests were carried out. The
raw current-time curves are shown in Fig. S3. The corresponding products, including the liquid and gas components were qualitatively and quantitatively analyzed. The results of the product
14
analysis indicate that the raw Cu foam and the nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes exhibit different ERCD activities, presenting a different variety of products. The products distribution and FE values of the different electrodes at different potentials are summarized in Fig. 6. As seen, the total FE of all electrodes for ERCD declines rapidly when the potential value approaches to -1.0 V, hence all the potentiostatic tests are terminated at this value. It can also be clearly seen that this deviation is resulted from HER, which is dynamically more active than

sections.heading: ERCD.
sections.text:
Moreover, one can conservatively conclude that the best potential range for ERCD on
these nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes ranges from -0.3 to -1.0 V. By comparing the
15
maximum total FE, it can be easily found that CuNS electrode shows the best performance with a total FE as high as 86.9% at -0.4 V; these features are competitive to the most reported Cu based catalysts. Analyzing in detail, the effect of onset potential for each product at each electrode can also be found from Fig. 6. As shown in Fig. 6a, only a small amount of formate is detected at the raw Cu foam electrode in the examined potential range, while in this case the maximum FE is only 5%, inferring that most of the applied current is just used for HER. This indicates that pure Cu foam has a very poor activity toward ERCD, but with an excellent formate selectivity.
Concerning the CuNW electrode (Fig. 6b), formate is firstly detected at -0.3 V, with a FE of
14.8%, meaning that the required overpotential for producing formate is only 50 mV [38]. Moreover, at CuNW electrode, formate is detected at all the investigated potentials and its corresponding FE varies only slightly. When the potential increases to -0.5 V, formate, acetic acid, methanol and ethanol are simultaneously detected. The FE of acetic acid is as high as 22.7%, while the FE values of methanol and ethanol are close to 3% and 11.5%, respectively. When the applied potential continues to increase, a rapid attenuation in FE caused by HER occurs. Simultaneously, a very small amount of CO and ethylene with the respective FE value close to about 0.2%, and less than 0.1% is detected at -0.7 V; the highest total FE at CuNW is 51.4% at -0.5 V.
At CuNS electrode (Fig. 6c), formate is firstly detected at -0.3 V, similar to that at CuNW
electrode, while acetic acid, methanol and ethanol are detected at -0.4 V. At this potential, the respective FE of formate, acetic acid, methanol and ethanol is 27.6%, 11.6%, 12.1%, and 35.7%, respectively; accordingly, the total FE is as high as 87%. With increasing the potential, the FE of the produced formate and methanol decreases slowly, while the respective FE values of acetic acid
16
and ethanol decreases rapidly. Moreover, except for CO, C2H4 and C2H6 are also detected at CuNS electrode among the ERCD products at -0.7 V with an FE around 0.2% for both (Table S1). As for CuNF electrode is concerned (Fig. 6d), the products distribution is similar to that observed at CuNS electrode. On the other hand, it is worth noting that the initial potential for C2 product generation is -0.3 V at CuNF electrode, which is more positive than that at CuNS electrode. The details of FE are summarized Table S1.
From the above results, it can be found that the products distribution of ERCD is heavily
dependent on both the applied potential and the micromorphology of the electrode. Further digging into the above results, one can find out that there is a sequence in the potential, at which a product is firstly detected, especially in the case of CuNW and CuNS electrodes. Formate is always the product that is firstly detected, followed by alcohols and then CO, while hydrocarbons are the last ones. It is widely accepted that the product generation sequence is closely related to the electron transfer process. Formate and CO generation from ERCD involves 2e- transfer pathways, which are obviously easier to proceed. On the other hand, alcohols and hydrocarbons generation from ERCD are multi-electron transfer processes, which are much more difficult to happen. The fact, that the potential at which CO is detected is more negative than that for alcohols at the nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes, arises from the stabilization of the transition state *CO species. Furthermore, the initial potential of C2 products generation shifts towards positive direction as the micro-topography of the nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes evolves from one to three dimensions. This implies that the high-dimensional morphology of Cu based electrodes is more favorable for C2 products formation from ERCD. This shift results from the unique micro-topographies of the nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes, which have a vital influence on the charge distribution of the reaction zone, affecting the final products generated [39-42]. Hence,
17
both the morphologies of the electrodes and electrolytes have effect on the stability of the intermediates, and thus the products distribution and FE are also affected. The above effect of the electrode morphology could be explained as follows. The reaction sites of CuNW are mainly located on the nanowires, where the active area of the wire field is small, making the unstable transition state products (unstable intermediates) easy to be desorbed, resulting in a low FE value. In the case of CuNS, the nanosheets consist of the main reaction location: i) disposing a larger surface area to accommodate a higher amount of active sites, ii) helping the stabilization of the intermediate products, and iii) facilitating the continuous reactions of the intermediates to produce high carbon products. As for CuNF is concerned, it is obtained from the further assembly of the stacking nanosheets, possessing similar properties to CuNS electrode, such as high carbon products. On the other hand, the stacking structure in CuNF could bury many active sites, resulting in a lower FE compared with CuNS electrode.
Except for electrode and the applied potential value, the electrolyte has also an obvious
effect on the ERCD performance. Based on the results of Fig. 7, the CuNS electrode, which exhibited the highest FE among the investigated electrodes as discussed above, was chosen for further investigation in two more electrolytes: a) 1.0 mol·L-1 KCl and b) 1.0 mol·L-1 KH2PO4 to investigate the effect of electrolyte. For comparison reasons, the experimental parameters were set the same, as the case above presented of 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3. As clearly seen in Fig. 7, in 1.0 mol·L-1 KCl electrolyte, the initial reduction potential of ERCD is about -0.4 V (Fig. 7a), while the LSV curves in N2 and CO2 saturated electrolytes almost overlap with each other in 1.0 mol·L-1 KH2PO4, indicating that ERCD is almost totally inhibited by HER (Fig. 7b).
18
can easily realize that much higher current density values are achieved in 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3 electrolyte (Fig. 5c) than that in the other two electrolytes (Fig. 7), indicating that at the as-prepared nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes, KHCO3 is more favorable for ERCD. Considering that the only difference, in these three electrolytes, is the released anion species, the observed differences in the LSV results could be resulted from the different interaction between the CuNS and the anion

In order to further check the electrolyte effect on ERCD, the potentiostatic tests were carried out.
In the case of 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3, the initial potential of CO, ethylene and ethane
generation are the same as those in 1.0 mol·L-1 KCl electrolyte. However, the FE of CO is much bigger than that in 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3. Further comparing the ERCD performances of CuNS electrode, in these three electrolytes, one can conclude that the CuNS electrode in the presence
20
of KHCO3 electrolyte exhibits the highest total FE and highest current density, promising a higher energy conversion. In KCl electrolyte, the total FE is less than that in KHCO3 and it is stable within a wide range of potential values. It is, however, surprisingly alcohols are firstly generated as the main product at low potential values, while formate is released at higher potential. This might be related to the special properties of Cl- ions that can act as the functional species and stabilize some intermediate products. These properties provide an expectation for controlling the product selectivity of ERCD at CuNS electrode. In 1.0 mol·L-1 KH2PO4, the released hydronium ions from the H2PO4 - hydrolysis facilitates HER and thus lead to ERCD suppression.
According to the above experimental results, it can be found that: i) there is a common
trend at the nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes as follows: the favorable potential for ERCD ranges from -1.0 V to about -0.3 V; ii) methane is not detected over all investigated potentials; iii) ethylene and ethane are usually produced at higher potentials; iv) all the examined electrodes show poor selectivity. Combining the above conclusions with the products distribution and the previous reports in the literature [43], the ERCD mechanism shown in Fig. 9 could be proposed.
Like in most ERCD steps, CO2 is firstly adsorbed onto the electrode surface to form
21
adsorptive CO2(ad) species. Part of CO2(ad) species receives an electron and then transforms into the transition state CO2 -(ad), part of which further reacts with the surrounding H+, generated from H2O, giving rise to the formation of formate. The other part of the transition state CO2 -(ad) is further hydrogenated to the transition state of CO*, which then converts into CO, when desorbed from the catalyst surface. CO* species are of crucial importance in the generation of the subsequent products, especially C2 products. Methanol is the result of CO* hydrogenation, in which only one CO* molecule is involved. For the formation of C2 products, two stable CO* species are required to isomerize, with simultaneous hydrogenation. In the ERCD process, formate is firstly obtained at low potential values, because of its short reaction path and the low kinetic resistance, compared with those of alcohols and especially C2 products. In the present work, methanol, acetic acid and ethanol are simultaneously obtained at the same potential. It might be considered that the nanostructured Cu electrode can stabilize both CO2 - (ad) and CO* transition states and the further hydrogenation and isomerization processes are promoted.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In the present work, nanostructured self-supporting Cu electrodes were prepared by a simple
solution immersion method followed by in-situ cyclic voltammetric treatments. The morphologies of the electrodes were strongly dependent on the oxidation time of Cu foam in the alkaline oxidizing agent, and three progressive microstructures of nanowires, nano-sheets and nano-flowers were controllably obtained along with the time increment. As the micromorphology evolves from nanowire to nanoflower, the initial potential for C2 products generation shifted to the positive direction. Among of these three electrodes, CuNS exhibited the highest FE for ERCD in 1.0 mol·L-1 KHCO3 electrolyte and multiple products can be produced at −0.4 V with a total FE of
22
up to 86.9%. The excellent performance of CuNS electrode might be benefited from the nanosheet structure, which could stabilize the intermediates. The anion species of electrolyte directly affected the performance of ERCD. The CuNS electrodes in different electrolytes exhibited very different onset potentials, FE and products distribution, which were directly related to the electrolyte properties. Moreover, Cl− ions can play a role in stabilizing intermediate products so that it can be used as the functional species to adjust the products distribution. It was the first time that the CuNS electrode was applied for ERCD with the advantages of low cost, simple synthesis, short preparation time, easy scale-up and high activity. Combined with the flexible control ability in FE and product distributions, CuNS electrode possesses great potential for the industrial application of ERCD.

sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text: The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (ERCD) was investigated on Cu electrodes. Nanostructured self-supported Cu electrode was controllably synthesized. The CuNS electrode exhibits low onset potential and high faraday efficiency in ERCD. The initial potential for C2 formation shifts positively from CuNW to CuNF electrode. The products distribution can be controlled by the electrolyte.
